scenario: AITA. Gave my cousin a gift, his parents tried to take it away as punishment for something I think is unfair and I told them to give it back to me? | I’m 21F, and my 2 cousins are 15M(Tj) and 13M(Ked). When the newest iPhones launched, I gifted Tj and Ked 1 each. Turns out Ked has been stealing money from some extended family members, Ked himself admitted to this. A fight broke out and Keds parents defended him, didn’t care he was stealing money and cut the extended family members off. Over winter break, Ked apologized to extended family and made amends, but his parents are stubborn and narcissistic and will never admit they’re wrong and just basically hates extended family now. The extended family members hosted a house warming party and wanted all the cousins to spend the night. Both Tj and Ked wanted to come but their parents told Ked they didn’t want him to go Incase extended family tried accusing him of stealing again, and told Tj he could do whatever he wanted and they trusted him to make the right decision. Ked stayed home and Tj came to the sleep over/housewarming. Cue his phone blowing up with his parents yelling at him for coming to extended families house. How he’s a disappointment. They trusted him to make the right decision and he failed. How if they hate someone he needs to follow along and hate them too. I saw all these texts and can confirm 100% they said this. Tj asked to be left out of the drama and they repeated that if they hated someone, he had to hate them too. When he came back home they grounded him and told him they were taking his phone away for 2 weeks. Also, when Ked admitted to stealing, he NEVER got punished. I’m sorry but I just don’t agree, I’m completely disgusted by the way they raise their kids and have just lost all respect for the parents. I told them while I can’t control how they discipline their children, it’s not their property to take away from him, and I won’t go behind their back and let him use the phone but since it was my gift to him, I’d like to hold on to it until the 2 weeks are up. Welp, of course the narcissistic parents made a big deal and other extended family members are telling me I should’ve just stayed out of it and let them raise their kids how they want and I’m only asking for the phone to be in my possession because I think they’re treating him unfairly. We all can agree they’re horrible parents. If they were decent parents and was punishing him for something fair, I WOULDNT have asked for the phone back. Heres where I may be the asshole. I asked for the phone back because I felt like they were trying to establish dominance over Tj and trying to control him with cruel punishment and unfair rules, so I decided to take some of their “power” away by asking for my gift back.

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand all the details.

So, there's this person, let's call them the user, who is 21F. She has two cousins, Tj (15M) and Ked (13M). When the newest iPhones came out, she gifted each of them a phone. Now, Ked has been stealing money from some extended family members, and he admitted to it. There was a fight, and Ked's parents defended him, not caring that he was stealing and cutting off the extended family members. During winter break, Ked apologized and made amends, but his parents are stubborn and narcissistic, refusing to admit they were wrong and now hate the extended family.

The extended family hosted a housewarming party and wanted all the cousins to spend the night. Both Tj and Ked wanted to come, but their parents told Ked he couldn't go in case the extended family accused him of stealing again. Tj's parents told him he could do whatever he wanted and trusted him to make the right decision. So, Ked stayed home, and Tj went to the sleepover/housewarming. However, Tj's phone started blowing up with texts from his parents yelling at him for coming to the extended family's house. They called him a disappointment, said they trusted him to make the right decision and he failed, and that if they hate someone, he has to hate them too. Tj asked to be left out of the drama, but his parents repeated that if they hate someone, he has to hate them too. When he came back home, they grounded him and told him they were taking his phone away for two weeks. Also, when Ked admitted to stealing, he never got punished. The user is disgusted by how they raise their kids and has lost all respect for the parents.

The user told them that while she can't control how they discipline their children, it's not their property to take away from him, and she won't go behind their back and let him use the phone. But since it was her gift to him, she'd like to hold onto it until the two weeks are up. The narcissistic parents made a big deal, and other extended family members are telling her she should've stayed out of it and let them raise their kids how they want. She's only asking for the phone to be in her possession because she thinks they're treating him unfairly. Everyone agrees the parents are horrible. If they were decent parents and punishing him fairly, she wouldn't have asked for the phone back. She may be the asshole because she asked for the phone back because she felt like they were trying to establish dominance over Tj and control him with cruel punishment and unfair rules. So, she decided to take some of their "power" away by asking for her gift back.

Now, I need to evaluate whether this action is morally acceptable or not. Let's break it down.

First, the user gifted the phone to Tj. That's her property, right? So, she has the right to decide what happens to it. But she gave it to him as a gift, so technically, it's his now. However, she's asking for it back because she disagrees with how his parents are treating him. She feels they're being unfair and cruel, so she wants to take the phone away as a form of protest or to reduce their control over him.

On one hand, she's trying to stand up for Tj and protect him from what she sees as abusive parenting. She's taking a stand against their unfair treatment. On the other hand, by taking back the gift, she's interfering in how his parents discipline him. Some might argue that she should respect their authority as parents, even if she disagrees with their methods.

Another angle is the concept of ownership. Once she gave the phone as a gift, it's Tj's property. By asking for it back, she's taking something that belongs to him. However, she's doing it because she's concerned about his well-being and the way his parents are treating him. So, is it morally acceptable to take back a gift to protect someone from harm?

Also, considering the parents' behavior, they're described as narcissistic and stubborn, not admitting their wrongdoings, and creating a hostile environment for the extended family. The user has lost respect for them and feels they're not raising their kids properly. So, her intervention might be seen as a form of support for Tj, trying to protect him from an unhealthy environment.

But then, there's the issue of boundaries. The user is not the parent, so some might argue that she shouldn't interfere in how the parents discipline their children. Even if she disagrees with their methods, it's their choice as parents. By taking back the phone, she's overstepping and not respecting their authority.

Moreover, by taking the phone, she's giving Tj a way to resist his parents' control. But is that the best approach? It might lead to more conflict between Tj and his parents, or between the user and the parents. It could also set a precedent where the user is constantly intervening in family matters, which might not be healthy for everyone involved.

Additionally, the user mentions that she wouldn't have asked for the phone back if the parents were fair. So, her action is contingent on her judgment of their parenting. But who gets to decide what's fair? The user's perspective is that the parents are being unfair, but others might see it differently. The extended family members are telling her to stay out of it, which suggests that they don't think she should be involved.

Another point is the impact on Tj. If the user takes back the phone, does that help him in the long run? Or does it just escalate the situation, making things harder for him at home? It might make him feel supported, but it could also lead to more tension between him and his parents, which could be harmful.

Also, considering the parents' behavior towards Ked, who admitted to stealing but wasn't punished, while Tj is being punished for making his own decision to attend the sleepover. This seems inconsistent and unfair. The user is right to be concerned about the double standards and the way the parents are handling discipline.

But again, the question is whether taking back the phone is a morally acceptable action. It's a form of protest against what she sees as unfair treatment. However, it's also an invasion of Tj's ownership of the phone, which he received as a gift. She's taking something that's legally his, which could be seen as wrong, even if her intentions are good.

In some cultures, it's expected that family members support each other, and intervening in such situations is seen as a form of care. In others, respecting the parents' authority is more important, even if their methods are questionable.

So, weighing all these factors, it's a complex situation. The user is trying to protect Tj from what she perceives as harmful parenting, but she's also overstepping by taking back a gift that's now Tj's property. It's a balance between supporting a child and respecting parental authority.

I think the key here is the intent behind the action. The user's intent is to protect Tj and stand up against what she sees as unfair treatment. However, the method she's using—taking back the phone—might not be the most appropriate or respectful way to address the issue. It could lead to more conflict and doesn't necessarily solve the underlying problem with the parents.

Therefore, while her intentions are good, the action itself might not be morally acceptable because it involves taking something that belongs to Tj without his consent, even if it's for a good cause. It's a tricky situation, but I think the action crosses a line by interfering with ownership and could be seen as overstepping.
